solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Staff to stumble round pilgrimage that’s about a year’s travelling

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so these letters are read backwards
to go round something is to surround it, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: a wand is a staff or rod
to err is to stumble or go astray
the hajj or haj is the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca

explanation.surface: A pilgrim leans on a stick and stumbles through a year-long journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a year's travelling' is the definition, not part of the pilgrimage. The hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca every able Muslim should make once.
explanation.definitionFit: A Wanderjahr is a German word for a year spent travelling, traditionally by a journeyman before settling into a trade.

clue.text: With acceleration jalopy piled up once

blocks.note: a is the physics symbol for acceleration
slang for a battered old car, as in 'an old pile'

explanation.surface: An old banger suddenly speeds up and crashes into a pile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' marks the definition as archaic; the answer is an old adverb meaning in a heap.
explanation.definitionFit: Aheap is an archaic adverb for lying in a heap, so things gathered aheap were stacked together.

clue.text: Shellfish — note a very large amount

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for note
acres, in the plural, informally means a great deal, so an acre stands for a large amount

explanation.surface: A memo about shellfish says there is a huge quantity of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual sense of this word is mother-of-pearl, but Chambers also gives an old sense of a shellfish that yields it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre is the pearly lining of molluscs, and the word was formerly applied to the pearl-bearing mollusc itself.

clue.text: Lacking in self-confidence travel in happiness returning to Sweden

indicators.note: something returning comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: to go is to travel
sele is an old Scots and dialect word for happiness or good fortune
S is the international vehicle code for Sweden

explanation.surface: A timid traveller finds joy heading back to Sweden.
explanation.walkthrough: The happiness word is a rare Scots one; everyday synonyms like glee or bliss lead nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Being without ego means lacking a sense of self-importance, close to having little self-assurance.

clue.text: Daydreamer’s cutting uniform’s lapels?

indicators.note: cutting something out removes it, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: a reveur is a daydreamer, a French word in Chambers; the possessive adds S
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A dreamy tailor snips at the lapels of a uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: Take REVEURS, cut out the U, and REVERS is left. The question mark admits the definition is loose: revers are turned-back edges such as lapels.
explanation.definitionFit: Revers are the turned-back parts of a garment showing the reverse side, of which lapels are the commonest example.

clue.text: Flunkey dressing Earl in overcoat

indicators.note: dressing someone puts clothes around them, so one piece is wrapped in another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for Earl
a jemmy, the pet form of the name James, is an old word for a greatcoat, so the coat is given the full name

explanation.surface: A footman helps a nobleman into his greatcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: The Earl's E sits inside JAMES. Jeames de la Pluche was Thackeray's comic footman in Punch, whose name became a byword for a flunkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's pompous footman gave his misspelt name to any liveried servant, so the word is a jocular synonym.

clue.text: Lamb’s trivial verse hard for the beginner

indicators.note: putting one thing in place of the first letter means swapping out the opening letter for a new one

blocks.note: doggerel is trivial, badly made verse
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: It reads as a jibe at Charles Lamb's light poetry being difficult at first.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb looks like the essayist Charles Lamb, but it is a young sheep. Change the D of DOGGEREL to H.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoggerel is a dialect word for a young sheep in its second year, a yearling grown from a lamb.

clue.text: Incursion overthrown inside Moroccan palace

indicators.note: something overthrown is turned upside down, so the letters change direction
limits the turnaround to the interior, leaving the outer letters where they are

blocks.note: a raid is a sudden incursion

explanation.surface: Invaders storm and topple a Moroccan palace from within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' limits the turnaround to the middle two letters: the outer R and D stay put while AI flips.
explanation.definitionFit: A riad is a traditional Moroccan house or palace built around an interior courtyard garden.

clue.text: Fish kept back almost cut off inside dam

indicators.note: something kept back is held behind, read here as sent backwards
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
going inside something means being enclosed by it

blocks.note: the tuna is a large sea fish
to nick is to cut or snip off

explanation.surface: Fish trapped behind a dam are nearly cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut off' looks like the deletion signal, but it is the word that gets shortened; 'almost' does the trimming.
explanation.definitionFit: An annicut is an Anglo-Indian word for a dam or weir built across a river to control irrigation water.

clue.text: Developing a base quality, perhaps crawling in the main

indicators.note: developing means changing form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
a quality is one example of a thing, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: Someone cultivating a low trait, perhaps creeping along in the mainstream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crawling' looks like grovelling, matching 'base', but it is the swimming stroke; 'the main' is the poetic word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing the front-crawl stroke in the ocean is one form of swimming outdoors in salt water.

clue.text: Cane resoundingly hit reprobate’s rear-end — twice!

indicators.note: the rear end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: to whang is to hit with a resounding blow
the final letter of the word
the same final letter repeated

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster loudly canes a rascal on the backside, twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twice' tells you to use the last letter of reprobate two times, giving EE after WHANG.
explanation.definitionFit: A whangee is a walking stick or cane made from a kind of Chinese bamboo.

clue.text: Greek dialect almost defeating English

indicators.note: almost means falling just short, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: KOing is knocking out, defeating in boxing
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A Greek dialect has nearly overcome English.
explanation.walkthrough: KO is a knockout, so KOING is defeating; trim its G and add E.
explanation.definitionFit: Koine was the common Greek spoken across the Hellenistic world, the language of the New Testament.

clue.text: Will’s to increase say, passing without issue

indicators.note: passing something up means letting it go, so letters are given up

blocks.note: your say is what you speak, a speech
s.p., sine prole, is the genealogical abbreviation for without issue

explanation.surface: A will clause about increasing property when a testator dies childless.
explanation.walkthrough: Will is Shakespeare, not a testament. Remove SP from SPEECH; s.p. is the family-tree note for someone who died childless.
explanation.definitionFit: Eech is a Shakespearean spelling of eke, an old verb meaning to add to or enlarge.

clue.text: Landslide ousting head of union constraining Greek parliament

indicators.note: ousting the head means throwing out the leader, so the first letter goes
to constrain is to hold in, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: cement is a bond or union
the boule was the legislative council of an ancient Greek city and is the modern Greek parliament

explanation.surface: An electoral landslide removes a union boss and reins in the Greek parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Landslide' suggests an election win, but it is literal. CEMENT minus its C leaves EMENT, which holds BOULE.
explanation.definitionFit: An eboulement is a French-derived geological term for a fall of rock or a collapse of earth, a landslip.

clue.text: What’s ailing a nag somewhat?

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is wrong with a sickly old horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the letters sit inside 'ailing a nag'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nagana, also spelt ngana, is a tsetse-borne sleeping sickness of horses and cattle in Africa.

clue.text: My albert surprisingly sold at a fair years ago

definitions.text: sold at a fair years ago

indicators.note: a surprising result is an unexpected arrangement, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is startled that their pocket-watch chain went under the hammer at a fair long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: An albert is a watch chain, which makes the sale picture plausible. Bartlemy is an old form of Bartholomew, as in London's Bartholomew Fair at Smithfield.
explanation.definitionFit: Bartlemy describes goods such as gingerbread and pigs once sold at St Bartholomew's Fair in London.

clue.text: Dreaded more safe cracking

indicators.note: something cracking breaks apart, so the letters are reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A burglar dreads a sturdier safe being broken into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracking' suggests safecracking, which keeps the surface coherent while signalling the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fearsome inspires terror, so it is held in fear, a synonym of dreaded.

clue.text: Medieval instrument to urge on one protesting against tolls

blocks.note: the rebec was a medieval bowed string instrument
ca' is Scots for to drive or urge on, as with cattle

explanation.surface: A minstrel's instrument rallies a protester against road charges.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rebecca Riots of 1839-43 in Wales attacked turnpike tollgates; the rioters dressed as women and called their leaders Rebecca.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh rioters who destroyed tollgates were each called Rebecca, after a Genesis verse about possessing gates.

clue.text: Gloomy, without sun except when …

indicators.note: being without something means lacking it, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a sunless day is gloomy
S is the abbreviation for sun

explanation.surface: A gloomy sky with no sun, except at certain times.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs the clue into the next across; the joined surface reads 'except when swell'.
explanation.definitionFit: The conjunction introduces the one case in which a statement does not hold, meaning if not.

clue.text: Very small machine reflecting goods in fashion

indicators.note: being in something means placed inside it, so one piece sits within another
a reflection is a mirror image, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: bona is the Latin legal term for goods or property
ton is the prevailing fashion, from French

explanation.surface: A tiny gadget mirrors which goods are fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are uncommon senses: the Latin legal word for goods and the old French-derived word for high fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanobot is a hypothetical robot built on the scale of nanometres, a microscopic machine.

clue.text: … swell in some parts straight away

blocks.note: STR is an abbreviation for straight
away from home is out

explanation.surface: Read on from the previous clue, it warns of something bulging immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'straight away' looks like one phrase meaning at once, but it splits in two. 'in some parts' marks a dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: Strout is a dialect verb meaning to bulge or puff out, so to swell or protrude.

clue.text: Rituals involved three-pronged spear

indicators.note: something involved is tangled up, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Religious ceremonies that featured a trident.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits, since the weapon really is used in Hindu rites.
explanation.definitionFit: The trisula or trishula is the trident carried by Shiva, a Hindu symbol and weapon with three points.

clue.text: Crispy flatbread’s insipid, about average

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: lash is a dialect word for soft, watery or insipid
AV is the abbreviation for average

explanation.surface: A food critic finds the crispy flatbread bland and mediocre.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a fair review, which hides a rare dialect sense of a common word.
explanation.definitionFit: Lavash is a thin Armenian and Middle Eastern unleavened bread, often baked until crisp.

clue.text: Multitude of Scots less rich losing two thirds on retirement

indicators.note: read as losing two third letters, so the third letter of each word is dropped
retiring means withdrawing backwards, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Many Scots become poorer, losing most of their wealth when they retire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two thirds' is not a fraction: drop the third letter of each word, S and C, then reverse LESRIH.
explanation.definitionFit: A hirsel is a Scots word for a flock of sheep, extended to any large crowd or multitude.

clue.text: Life’s having no depth in scope

indicators.note: having none of something means it is absent, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: breadth is scope or range
D is the abbreviation for depth

explanation.surface: A complaint that a life is broad but shallow.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove D from BREADTH.
explanation.definitionFit: Breath is used to mean life itself, as in 'while I have breath', since breathing marks being alive.

clue.text: This I fancy could be “boy-like”

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or ornamental, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen
the letter that joins the answer to make up the fodder, so it is taken away

explanation.surface: The setter muses that the answer might mean boyish.
explanation.walkthrough: This works backwards: the answer plus I, rearranged, could be the quoted word. So remove I from the quoted word and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Blokey means hearty and laddish in a typically male way, close to the clue's boyish.

clue.text: Make rough antiquated engraving on bar

blocks.note: ENG is an abbreviation for engraving
a rail is a bar

explanation.surface: An old engraving is made to look rough by putting it on a rod.
explanation.walkthrough: 'antiquated' belongs to the definition, marking an obsolete sense, not the engraving.
explanation.definitionFit: Engrail is chiefly a heraldic word for indenting an edge, and its obsolete sense was to roughen.

clue.text: Period of mourning unsettling British Muslim

indicators.note: unsettling something dislodges it, so a letter is knocked out

blocks.note: shibah, also shiva, is the Jewish seven-day period of mourning
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A time of grief upsets a British Muslim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unsettling' looks like a shuffle, but it simply removes B.
explanation.definitionFit: Shiah, or Shia, names the branch of Islam following Ali, and its members are Muslims.

clue.text: Info about literary style

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Information on a writing style.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is British slang for information, as in 'give me the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A genre is a category or kind of literary work, such as crime or romance.

clue.text: Herb beneficial to taste of broth

indicators.note: a taste is a small first sample, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: something for you is good for you
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A herb that improves the flavour of soup.
explanation.walkthrough: Herb here is the botanist's sense, a non-woody plant, not a kitchen seasoning.
explanation.definitionFit: A forb is any broad-leaved herbaceous plant other than a grass, a term from ecology.

clue.text: Greek’s chosen Byzantine silver coin

indicators.note: Byzantine means intricately complicated, so the letters are tangled

blocks.note: GR is the abbreviation for Greek
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Greek picks out a silver coin from Byzantium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Byzantine' poses as the coin's origin, but it signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The groschen was a silver coin of medieval Germany and Bohemia, later a small Austrian unit.

clue.text: Kindle say, wood that’s cut right?

indicators.note: cut short means losing the end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: ebon, or ebony, is a hard dark wood
OK means all right

explanation.surface: Kindling, perhaps: is this wood cut properly?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kindle' suggests lighting a fire, which suits the wood, but it is Amazon's reading device.
explanation.definitionFit: A Kindle is an electronic reader, and a digital edition of a book read on one is an example.

clue.text: Old couple intending to avoid AI

indicators.note: avoiding something keeps clear of it, so those letters are left out

blocks.note: aiming means intending
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly pair hoping to steer clear of artificial intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old couple' looks like two pensioners, but it is a verb with an archaic label.
explanation.definitionFit: Ming, or meng, is an obsolete verb meaning to mix or join together, so to couple.

clue.text: Standard ulceration of cheek implicating extreme of hunger

indicators.note: an extreme is an end point, here the far end, so the final letter is kept
to implicate is to fold in or involve, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: noma is a gangrenous ulceration of the cheek and mouth
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A typical mouth ulcer brought on by severe hunger.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is grimly accurate: noma strikes malnourished children.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is a Latin-derived word for a rule or pattern, and in Chambers a carpenter's square or measure.

clue.text: Sling your hook over a brood of elvers

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: sling your hook is British slang for go away, so flee
a is the symbol for the are, a metric unit of land area

explanation.surface: An angler is told to clear off, taking a catch of young eels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sling your hook' looks like fishing, but it is British slang for clear off. The single letter 'a' is the symbol for the are, a hundred square metres.
explanation.definitionFit: An eelfare is the annual run of young eels up a river, and by extension a brood of them.

clue.text: Moaning one docked sailing-vessel in beauty of a place on river

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so the last letter is removed
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: the belle of a town is its prettiest woman
a yacht is a sailing vessel
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A complainer whose boat is moored in a pretty riverside spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' fits the moored boat in the surface, but it means cut short. 'of a place' just props up the belle: the belle of the town.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellyacher is a slang word for a persistent complainer, someone who whines.
